summary.text: 吃 is a phonosemantic character: 口 supplies a speech-related meaning category, and the right-hand element supplies sound. Its earliest supported sense is halting speech; the familiar sense “eat” has a distinct history whose relationship to the speech sense and to 喫 remains unresolved.

formation.text: The character combines 口, associated here with speech, and a phonetic element. The older analysis identifies that element as 气; the modern right side is written like 乞. The exact graphic path between these forms within 吃 is unresolved.

components.text: 口 is the left-hand mouth component. Here it contributes the speech-related meaning category; its own pictographic history does not make it a depiction within 吃.

The modern right side is written like 乞, while the older analysis names 气 as the sound element. 乞 and 气 share an earlier graph in their separate history, but the dated graphic path within 吃 is unresolved.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese, 吃 is reconstructed as *kɯd and 乞 as *kʰɯd(s). These forms are similar enough to support a sound-series relation, though they are not identical; modern Mandarin chī and qǐ differ.

history.text: The received Shuowen analysis records the structure 从口气聲 and defines 吃 as difficult or halting speech. A transmitted Shiji passage also describes Han Fei as 口吃, supporting this speech sense. Neither establishes the earliest physical form of the whole graph.

The familiar eating use is associated with both 吃 and 喫, but accounts disagree about its earliest spelling and how the graphs relate. Interchange, sound borrowing and simplification have been proposed; no sequence is established.

uncertainties.text: The earliest physical attestation of 吃 is unresolved; no inspected primary paleographic evidence establishes an oracle-bone or bronze form. Reported Warring States ceramic and Western Han manuscript examples remain unverified leads.
The Shuowen analysis names 气, while the modern right side resembles 乞. The separate history of 乞 and 气 is described, but the dated graphic changes within 吃 are not traced.
The earliest eating examples and the relationship among 吃, 喫, 齕 and related forms remain disputed. Literary citation dates do not establish the dates of surviving physical witnesses.

senses.period: attested in the received Shiji text; physical witness dating unresolved
senses.text: The Shuowen entry defines 吃 as difficult or halting speech, and the transmitted Shiji passage describes Han Fei as 口吃. This supports the speech sense, not an eating sense.
Dictionaries record 吃 for eating or drinking and associate this use with 喫. Its earliest spelling and relation to the speech sense remain unsettled.

senses.period: dating unresolved for 吃; Yuan-text examples are reported for 喫
senses.text: “Suffer” and “endure” are recorded glosses for 吃; Yuan-text examples are reported specifically for 喫. The chronology and semantic path to 吃 are not established here.
吃 is commonly used for “eat”; “drink” is also recorded. Its relation to the older speech sense remains unresolved.

limitations.text: The relationship between the eating use and the speech word is unresolved: the sources do not determine whether it arose through semantic development, borrowing between graphs for similar-sounding words, or a separate graphic history. No developmental chain is asserted.
Additional senses include absorbing, consuming, swallowing chess pieces and undergoing, but their chronology is insufficient to connect them reliably to the earliest attested sense.

overview.text: 吃 combines a mouth-related meaning element with a sound element. Its earliest supported meaning is halting speech; the familiar “eat” sense has a separate, disputed history.

components.text: 口 contributes the speech-related meaning category in 吃.
The modern right side is written like 乞; the older analysis names 气. Their exact graphic connection within 吃 is unresolved.

takeaway.text: 吃 means “eat” today, but how this use relates to the older stammer sense and to 喫 remains unresolved.

relationships.text: 口 contributes the speech-related semantic category in the traditional phonosemantic analysis.
The older analysis names 气 as the sound element; the modern right side resembles 乞, and historical pronunciation comparison supports a sound-series relation.
The traditional analysis explicitly names 气 as the sound element in 吃.
